function.description: Send a GET request to a specified URL to retrieve all products and branches with triangulation runs in the latest 90 days. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to send the GET request to.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The MIME types that are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request as a dictionary of header names to header values.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

days.description: The number of days to look back for triangulation runs.

end_date.description: The end date for the data retrieval period, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'. If null, defaults to the current date.

params.description: Optional query parameters to include in the request.

auth.description: HTTP authentication credentials as a (username, password) tuple.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: Proxy settings as a dictionary mapping protocol names to URLs of the proxies.

stream.description: If true, the response should be streamed; otherwise, the response will be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not.

**Triangulation metrics** are quantitative indicators that describe the quality, performance, and characteristics of a triangulation run—typically a computational process that converts a set of points (e.g., GPS observations, sensor readings, or survey markers) into a network of triangles (a Delaunay triangulation, Voronoi diagram, or other spatial tessellation). These metrics help analysts, engineers, and scientists evaluate how well the triangulation meets their objectives, whether it’s for mapping, interpolation, mesh generation, or geodetic analysis. Below is a quick‑look at the most common categories of triangulation metrics and why they matter: | Category | Typical Metric(s) | What It Tells You | |----------|-------------------|-------------------| | **Geometric Quality** | • **Triangle aspect ratio** (ratio of longest side to shortest side)
• **Minimum/maximum angle**
• **Circumradius‑to‑edge‑length ratio** | Indicates how “well‑shaped” triangles are. Poorly shaped triangles (very skinny or obtuse) can degrade numerical stability and interpolation accuracy. | | **Coverage & Completeness** | • **Area covered** (total area of all triangles)
• **Untriangulated gaps** (areas not covered by any triangle)
• **Edge density** (average number of edges per unit area) | Shows how thoroughly the domain has been triangulated and whether there are holes that might affect downstream analyses. | | **Error & Accuracy** | • **Residual error** (difference between observed and predicted values at vertices)
• **Root‑mean‑square error (RMSE)**
• **Maximum absolute error** | Quantifies how closely the triangulation fits the underlying data. Lower errors usually mean higher fidelity. | | **Computational Performance** | • **Run time** (seconds/minutes)
• **Memory usage**
• **Number of iterations** (for iterative refinement algorithms) | Helps assess algorithm efficiency and scalability. | | **Topological Consistency** | • **Number of connected components**
• **Presence of dangling nodes**
• **Edge crossing count** | Ensures the mesh is topologically sound (no overlapping edges, no isolated nodes). | | **Statistical Distribution** | • **Histogram of triangle areas**
• **Cumulative distribution of edge lengths** | Provides insight into the variability of the mesh, which can influence interpolation smoothness and computational load. | ### Why Triangulation Metrics Matter 1. **Quality Assurance** – Before using a mesh for simulation, interpolation, or visualization, you want to confirm that it meets minimum geometric standards. 2. **Comparative Analysis** – When you run multiple triangulation algorithms or tweak parameters, metrics let you objectively compare results. 3. **Error Propagation** – In geodetic or hydrological modeling, knowing the residual error helps predict how inaccuracies in the mesh will affect final outputs. 4. **Optimization** – Performance metrics guide decisions about algorithm choice, hardware requirements, and parallelization strategies. 5. **Regulatory Compliance** – Some industries (e.g., civil engineering, environmental monitoring) require documented mesh quality thresholds. ### How the `requests_get` Function Relates The `requests_get` function you mentioned is designed to pull data on *products* and *branches* that have undergone triangulation runs in the last 90 days. While the function itself just fetches raw data, the returned dataset typically includes fields that can be used to compute the metrics above—such as: - Number of triangles generated - Total area covered - Residual errors reported by the triangulation engine - Run time and resource usage logs Once you have that data, you can feed it into a post‑processing script (Python, R, MATLAB, etc.) to calculate the metrics listed in the table and generate visualizations (heat maps, histograms, error plots). --- #### Quick Example (Python) ```python import requests import pandas as pd # Call the API resp = requests.get( url="https://api.example.com/triangulation", params={"days": 90}, headers={"Accept": "application/json"} ) data = resp.json() # Convert to DataFrame df = pd.DataFrame(data["runs"]) # Compute simple metrics df["aspect_ratio"] = df["max_side"] / df["min_side"] df["rmse"] = (df["residuals"]**2).mean()**0.5 print(df[["run_id", "aspect_ratio", "rmse"]].head()) ``` This snippet demonstrates how you might start turning raw API output into actionable metrics. --- **Bottom line:** Triangulation metrics give you a concise, quantitative snapshot of how well your triangulation performed—geometrically, computationally, and in terms of data fidelity. They’re essential for validating meshes, comparing algorithms, and ensuring that downstream analyses rest on a solid foundation.
